segs.text: Section fifteen. Pulmonary toxicity. For each organ she asks why the whole organ is susceptible and why certain parts of it are. The lungs are exposed because we breathe all the time, and they carry an oxidative burden. We breathe in oxygen and pollutants carrying reactive oxygen species, such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides. White blood cells that come in to fight pathogens or clean up damaged tissue release more. The result damages the fats and proteins of lung cells.

For a gas, the property that matters is water solubility, not size, because it decides how far down the gas goes. She said very hydrophilic gases go far down into the lungs and hydrophobic gases do not. For particles, size, shape and breathing pattern decide where they deposit, and heavier breathing, jogging rather than walking, brings in more. Clearance by coughing and by the cilia of the upper airway decides how long particles stay. Because deposition depends on what was inhaled, the site of lung damage points back to the likely cause.

Very small particles are so light they are breathed back out. Large particles come in fast, cannot turn the curve into the next branch, and impact the upper airway where the bronchioles bifurcate. Medium particles are heavy enough not to be breathed out and small enough to go around the curves, so in the pause at the end of a breath in, they settle in the alveolar regions. She said, the medium sized particles are the ones that are the most concerning. Long, thin, sharp asbestos fibers embed at the upper bifurcations, and some move through the tissue and cause mesothelioma on the outer lining of the lungs.

Acute responses are airway reactivity, where bronchoconstriction narrows the airway and causes wheezing, coughing, chest tightness and dyspnea, and pulmonary edema, which thickens the alveolar-capillary barrier. Chronic responses are fibrosis, emphysema, where the lungs become too plastic and trap air, and asthma. Asthma is on her chronic list even though attacks are sudden. Fluorine gas, chlorine gas and the other halogens give acute responses, because they are very caustic with the water in the lungs.

Pulmonary toxicity does not require inhalation. Bleomycin and cyclophosphamide, chemotherapy drugs given intravenously, and the herbicides monocrotaline and paraquat reach the lungs through the blood and cause pulmonary fibrosis. She said, we give them by I V, but they're known to cause pulmonary toxicity. This is pulmonary toxicity by location, while fibrosis itself stays non-organ specific by its mechanism.
